title: Board texture
summary: Dry and wet boards: whom the flop suits better.

dry-wet.text:
**Board texture** is how connected the cards on the table are. It decides how many made hands and draws players have and how to bet.

- A **dry** board: different suits, ranks far apart, for example K♠ 7♦ 2♣. Few draws: whoever is ahead now usually stays ahead.
- A **wet** board: suits and ranks connect, for example J♥ T♥ 8♣. Lots of straight and flush draws, and the balance shifts card by card.

advantage.text:
**Range advantage** is which player has more strong hands on this board. The preflop raiser holds more high cards and pairs (AA, KK, AK), so boards with an ace or a king, like K♠ 7♦ 2♣, favor them. A big blind call holds more middling and small hands, so boards like 8♠ 7♦ 6♣ suit it more often.

**Nut advantage** is who has more of the very strongest hands (sets, straights). It lets that player bet big.

q-wet.explain: 9-8-6 with two hearts gives lots of straight draws (T7, 75, JT) and flush draws, so it is wet.

t1.q: Why is the next card less scary on a dry board?
options: Few draws: the hand ahead now usually stays ahead
You cannot bet on a dry board
A dry board always means a split
t1.explain: A dry board has almost no draws, so later cards rarely change who is ahead.

t2.q: Board A♠ K♦ 4♣. Who usually has the range advantage?
t2.explain: The raiser holds more aces and kings (AA, KK, AK, AQ), so a high board is theirs.

t3.q: What is the board Q♥ 7♥ 3♥ called?
t3.explain: Three cards of one suit make a monotone board: anyone with a heart already has a flush draw.
